column2: The Lord's speech introduces offerings after entry into the land.
The promised land is explicitly the land of their dwelling and God's gift. The conditional entry clause continues into the offering instructions.
Whole offerings, sacrifice, vow, willingness and festivals all remain, with cattle and sheep as the animal categories.
column3: The breadth of the flock term merits consistency review; no global livestock substitution is made.

column2: The presenter brings one tenth of an oiphi of flour with one quarter hin of oil. Both fractions and units remain.
One quarter hin of wine accompanies each lamb. The selected closing offering-and-savour clause is retained.
A ram requires two tenths of flour and one third hin of oil, for either whole burnt offering or sacrifice.
The ram's wine measure is also one third hin, presented for sweet savour.
The cattle case includes whole burning, a vow sacrifice or deliverance. The sentence continues into the calf's quantities.
The calf receives three tenths of flour and half a hin of oil; the selected third-person presenter remains he.
Half a hin of wine accompanies the calf, matching its oil measure.
The per-animal rule names calf, ram and lamb, followed by sheep or goats. The unusual lamb-from-goats wording is not silently normalized.
column3: The scope of the final animal categories requires syntactic review.

column2: The quantity scales with the number prepared, explicitly applying to each one. Repetition is retained.
Every native follows the same offering procedure, with sweet savour as its stated purpose.
The sojourner clause extends across generations; the selected final subject is the congregation, not a silently substituted he.
column3: The transition from the individual sojourner to congregation needs fuller discourse review.

column2: One enduring law applies to people and attached sojourners, with the same standing before the Lord.
One law and one ordinance are both stated for native and sojourner, without collapsing the two terms.
A new divine speech introduces the dough portion.
The Lord brings them into the land; the entry condition precedes eating its bread.
Eating the land's loaves occasions a portion set apart for the Lord. The gift/set-apart language remains.
A firstfruits loaf from dough is compared with a threshing-floor portion. The analogy is not converted into a specified percentage.
The firstfruits-of-dough phrase continues, with giving to the Lord throughout generations.
Erring and not performing all the commandments introduce the inadvertence case; the scope is not reduced to one named command.
Commands through Moses extend from the original command day into later generations.
Unintentional action outside the assembly's sight calls for an unblemished calf, its accompanying offerings and one sin goat. The whole congregation acts.
Priestly atonement and forgiveness are grounded in inadvertence and the offered gift; the repeated unintentional language remains.
Forgiveness includes the entire congregation and sojourner because the whole people's act was unintentional.
The individual case requires one year-old female goat. Sex, age and number remain explicit.
The priest makes atonement for the inadvertent sinner, with the repeated atonement expression. No additional forgiveness sentence is imported into the selected verse.
Native and sojourner share one law for inadvertent action, distinct from the following defiant case.
A presumptuous hand characterizes the deed; either native or sojourner can provoke God and be destroyed from the people.

Worthless treatment of the word and scattering the commandments explain emphatic destruction. The proposal retains the selected in him for the concluding sin expression instead of the inherited upon him.
In the wilderness the people find a man gathering wood on the Sabbath. The act and day remain specific.
The finders bring the man to Moses, Aaron and the whole assembly. The Sabbath and wood-gathering details repeat.
Custody follows because they had not determined what to do. The selected active deliberation is retained.
The divine command prescribes death by the whole congregation's stoning; the emphatic death construction remains.
The congregation takes him out and stones him; both outside-camp phrases remain. No separate death-result clause is added from another text.
A new divine speech introduces the garment fringes.
Fringes belong at garment corners for generations, with a blue thread. The instruction shifts from let them make to you shall put, as in the Greek.
Seeing the fringes prompts remembrance and action; following thoughts and eyes is forbidden under the whoring image. All commandments remains explicit.
Remembrance, obedience to all commands and holiness to God state the purpose.
The divine self-identification appears twice around the Egypt-deliverance purpose. Both occurrences remain.
Korah speaks in the selected opening, with his Levitical genealogy and the named Reubenite associates. No took construction is substituted.
The 250 men are assembly leaders, council members and renowned men; all three descriptions remain.
The challengers assert universal congregational holiness and divine presence, then question Moses and Aaron's rising against it. Their charge remains direct speech.
Moses' immediate response on hearing is to fall face down.
The selected verbs describe God's having visited/known and brought near His own and the holy. No tomorrow-morning test is inserted into this verse.
Korah and his whole congregation are instructed to take fire pans.
Fire and incense are placed tomorrow; the Lord's chosen man is holy. The closing enough addresses Levi's sons.
Moses addresses Korah while summoning all Levi's sons to listen.
The question challenges treating Levitical separation, nearness, tent service and service to the congregation as too little.
Korah and all his Levitical brothers have been brought near; seeking priestly service is the further demand challenged.
The gathering is against God, while the question about Aaron exposes the complaint's target. No new rank is assigned to Aaron here.
Dathan and Abiram, sons of Eliab, refuse Moses' summons. Their refusal is retained as direct speech.
The speakers call their former land milk-and-honey land and accuse Moses of killing and ruling them. The inversion remains their rhetoric.
The selected even-if construction about entering good land and receiving fields precedes the gouged-eyes allegation. It is not changed to a straightforward negative about failed entry.
column3: The counterfactual construction and its eye-image require further syntax and apparatus review.

column2: Moses is deeply distressed and asks that their sacrifice not be attended to. The selected desirable possession is retained rather than substituted with donkey.
Consecrating Korah's congregation and being ready tomorrow are explicit instructions, including Aaron in the meeting.
There are 250 fire pans plus the separately addressed Korah and Aaron instructions. Each man's pan remains his own.
The men prepare fire and incense; the selected final standing subjects are Moses and Aaron at the tent entrances.
Korah assembles his whole group against them and the Lord's glory appears to the whole congregation.
The Lord addresses Moses and Aaron before commanding separation.
Separation precedes the threatened immediate consumption. All at once is temporal English for the single decisive action, not an added count.
Both leaders fall face down and invoke God twice, as God of spirits and all flesh. One man's sin is contrasted with anger at the whole assembly.
The next divine speech addresses Moses alone.
The command names Korah's congregation as the group to withdraw from; other names are not imported into this selected verse.
Moses goes to Dathan and Abiram accompanied by all Israel's elders.
Separation from the stubborn men's tents and avoiding all their possessions prevent sharing destruction in their sin.
Withdrawal is from Korah's tent; Dathan and Abiram stand with wives, children and the final baggage term.
column3: The final collective's range between baggage and household dependants needs lexical review.

column2: The coming sign establishes divine sending for all these works, denying Moses as their independent origin.
Ordinary human death and visitation would disprove Moses' commission. The negative conclusion remains conditional.
A divine portent opens earth's mouth to swallow households, tents and possessions alive into Hades. All listed objects and the conclusion about provocation remain.
The ground splits beneath them when Moses finishes all his words; the timing is explicit.
Earth swallows the people, households, everyone with Korah and livestock. The selected livestock is not generalized away as possessions.
Living descent to Hades, earth covering them and perishing from the assembly remain three connected statements.
All nearby Israel flees at the cry, fearing the earth might swallow them too. The final fear is expressed as a lest clause.
Fire from the Lord consumes the 250 incense offerers, closing the selected chapter at verse 35.
